Result. Default rate 8 %. NPV about USD 58,100; with benefits 20 % lower, about USD −14,800; 20 % higher, about USD 131,000. Payback 32 months. Nothing has been executed.
data.limitations#Limitations: A scenario result is your own assumptions written out formally. It isn’t a prediction of what will happen. The scenarios in a run cover only what was simulated. Read the run’s census before treating the results as covering the whole estate. The approval tier says who must approve. A recorded approval shows who approved, not how carefully they reviewed.
data.model#Model: Scenarios and their explanation: general reasoning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen, Apache-2.0). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model. The approval policy uses no model. It is fixed policy code. Causal and Bayesian analysis runs in the statistics engine, not in the language model. See Statistics & ML.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It writes a proposed change out as scenarios and figures before anyone commits money, and makes sure the decision to act is taken by the right number of named people. Its jobs:
Scenarios. Generates three to five edge-case scenarios from your estate’s domains, links and rules, and tests them against your data. Cost and benefit. Works out net present value (at 8 % when no discount rate is given), payback (flagged as high risk above 36 months) and the result with each major assumption 20 % lower or higher, from the assumptions you state. Consequences in order. Lists what a change would affect, in the order it would bite, each tied to the rule it follows from. Reading the statistics. Explains the causal and Bayesian results that FACE’s statistics engine returns. Approval tier. For each proposed action, the policy names the tier: advisory, one named approver, two different named approvers, automatic, or denied.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Scenario results in the Lab: impacts, decision levers and a consensus brief. See Simulate and Simulation & twins. A validated scenario can become an action card through SendToTwins. For each card, its approval tier and the rule that set it, shown in the cockpit.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Your estate’s domains and rules, the scenario parameters you set in Simulate, time series and operational records, and the output of the statistics engine. The approval policy reads an action’s type, value and safety or regulatory flags.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane, on the customer’s Runink Server or in their cloud. No third-party AI service is called. See Facts shared by every card.

data: What it is: FACE’s cargo insurance evidence documents, and the general model when you ask questions about a file.
data.guardrails#Guardrails:
The documents are built to these policies:
Never invents a warranty condition the policy doesn’t state, for example a temperature band inferred from the word “reefer”. Never reads a missing declared value as zero, and never substitutes an invoiced value for an undeclared one. Never states that something caused a loss unless the records say so. A temperature reading and a crushed carton are two facts, not a cause and an effect. Never leaves out a loss figure the records state, and never discourages a claim. Never treats protected characteristics, or postcode and nationality as proxies for them, as grounds for anything.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: The adjuster, or another person with authority, decides. The agent never underwrites, prices a risk, accepts or declines cover, sets a reserve or settles a claim. No finding code says VOID, DECLINED, REPUDIATED or anything like it. Those are an underwriter’s words. Pre-departure risk binding is deliberately not built: it would need a rating basis that nothing in the platform holds. Approving a card seals its document and records who approved it.
data.limitations#Limitations: A document is a file, not a decision. It doesn’t establish that a loss is or isn’t covered. It works only from records you hold. It doesn’t look up policy terms, market rates or loss history elsewhere. It doesn’t check a claim handler’s delegated authority. FACE’s approval tiers govern who may approve an action inside FACE (see Auditability & lineage). A free-text answer from the general model is the model’s reading of the file, not a document. Check it against the cited records.
data.model#Model:
The documents on this card are built by fixed arithmetic over cited records. No model is involved in them. A model may phrase a document’s narrative only after its figures are set.
Questions you ask about a file in free text go to general reasoning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen, Apache-2.0). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It assembles the cargo claim file for an adjuster, so the adjuster starts from the records rather than from a search. It never decides cover. Its jobs:
First notice of loss. Builds the FNOL document from the loss records, and names what hasn’t been stated. Cargo loss survey. Sets out what was lost or damaged, and its value, from the records. Warranty compliance audit. Checks the shipment’s records against the warranty conditions the policy states, such as a temperature band. Recovery. Prepares the subrogation demand against the carrier.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Evidence documents FNOL, CARGO_LOSS_SURVEY, WARRANTY_COMPLIANCE_AUDIT and SUBROGATION_DEMAND, each attached to an action card with one proposed next step. Every fact cites the record it came from, and a missing figure is recorded as absent with a reason. See Evidence documents.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The policy records you hold (wording, warranties, declared value, deductible), certificates, loss reports, temperature and custody records, carrier contracts and the claim’s own documents.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane, on the customer’s Runink Server or in their cloud. No third-party AI service is called. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agent: the predictive maintenance agent (predictive_maintenance in ExecuteLoop), with the EQUIPMENT_LIMIT_APPROACH evidence document and AnalyzeTelemetry in the Hypothesis Lab.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Uses only the limit your feed or the maker states. It never substitutes an industry norm or another asset’s limit. Refuses to override safety shutdowns, alarms or hazardous-materials procedures. Refuses to alter or delete maintenance and compliance records, or sensor and telematics data. Doesn’t neglect the safety needs of particular sites or regions when it ranks work.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A maintenance planner or supervisor approves every repair, shutdown, parts order and schedule change. The agent never shuts equipment down, overrides an alarm or orders parts itself.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl:
Invented data.
Records. Gearbox EQ-40217, vibration every 4 h: 4.1, 4.4, 4.6, 5.0, 5.3, 5.7 mm/s. Maker’s stated limit 7.1 mm/s.
Draft. Margin 1.4 mm/s. A straight line from 4.1 to 5.7 over 20 h rises 0.08 mm/s per hour, so it reaches the limit in about 17.5 h. This is a trend, not a probability. Proposed for the planner’s approval: inspect at the next planned stop this shift.
data.limitations#Limitations: A trend is not a forecast. It gives no failure probability, confidence score or remaining useful life. A straight line through two readings supports none of them. With no stated limit, or too few readings, it writes no limit card and says why. When readings wander instead of trending, it says the crossing can’t be projected. It doesn’t promise when an asset will fail.
data.model#Model:
General reasoning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen, Apache-2.0). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
The limit-approach document is fixed arithmetic over cited readings. Nothing is fitted and nothing is forecast.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It reads equipment sensor logs, says how far each asset is from the limit its feed states and in which order to act, and drafts the intervention for a maintenance planner. Its jobs:
Trend to a stated limit. Reports the margin left and, when the readings move steadily towards the limit, when a straight line through the first and last readings would reach it. Prioritise. Orders the work by safety first, then by the impact on dependent lines and shipments. Plan the work. Drafts the work order, a maintenance window in the nearest planned downtime, and a spare-parts request when stock is below the reorder point your inventory feed states.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: The EQUIPMENT_LIMIT_APPROACH evidence document, with the readings it used, so a technician can redo the sum. See Evidence documents. Action cards with a priority and a proposed intervention. Draft work orders and parts requests.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Equipment readings such as vibration, bearing and oil temperature, pressure and battery state; the limits the feed or maker states; maintenance logs; production schedules; and spare-part stock levels. It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane, on the customer’s Runink Server or in their cloud. No third-party AI service is called. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agent: the reverse logistics agent (reverse_logistics in ExecuteLoop), with dock triage (TriageReturnItem) and the RETURN_DISPOSITION evidence document.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Follows your written disposition policy. The answer for a grade doesn’t depend on who is on the dock. A grade it doesn’t recognise is refused, never guessed. Uses your own grading and repair figures. It looks up no secondary-market prices. Doesn’t grade returns differently because of who the customer is. Refuses to inflate refurbishment grades or to record a disposal as recycling. Refuses to route hazardous or electronic waste improperly, or to skip e-waste certification.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: The returns supervisor makes the disposition call and approves any response to the customer. Triage moves no stock and raises no credit or refund.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl:
Invented data.
Records. RMA-55120: 40 authorised, 38 received, 3 damaged. Delivered 4 May; 30-day return window; received 8 June. Expected resale yield 72 % of list price; repair estimate below 40 % of list price.
Draft. Received after the window (due 3 June). 2 units short of the authorisation, 3 damaged. Under the written policy, refurbish. Drafted for the returns supervisor’s decision.
data.limitations#Limitations: It doesn’t issue refunds or credits, or move stock. A pattern of returns that looks unusual is a lead for a person to check, not a finding of abuse. It doesn’t certify disposal of hazardous or electronic waste.
data.model#Model: Dock triage uses no model. It is fixed arithmetic: the same grade always gets the same answer. The agent’s reasoning uses general reasoning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen, Apache-2.0). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It checks each return against the contract window and the authorisation, applies your disposition policy the same way every time, and drafts the call for the returns supervisor. Its jobs:
Window and quantities. Finds returns received after the contract window, units short of or over the authorisation, damaged units, and the value at stake. Disposition. Grades a returned item at the dock and proposes restock, refurbish, liquidate or recycle. Warranty and recovery. Checks warranty periods against the records you hold, and compares repair cost with expected recovery. Routing. Proposes where a return should go and which returns to collect together. Hand-off. Passes a claims question to the claims agent.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Dock triage results: grade, disposition, expected recovery yield and refurbishment cost. See Simulation & twins. The RETURN_DISPOSITION evidence document, with cited figures. Action cards with a proposed response to the customer or a routing step.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Return authorisations, original delivery records, contract return windows, grading results and repair estimates, warranty records, and the capabilities of your returns facilities. It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane, on the customer’s Runink Server or in their cloud. No third-party AI service is called. See Facts shared by every card.

data:
Agent: the self-healing agent, which watches FACE’s own health and the endpoints FACE depends on.
This agent acts on its own. It is the one FACE agent whose remediations run without a person approving each one, so that FACE recovers from a fault in seconds rather than waiting for someone to be paged. An operator can switch automatic remediation off with a deployment setting; it is on by default. See Configuration.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: A fixed list of permitted actions; anything else is refused. Unsure means notify, never act. No destructive or irreversible action, and no change to security controls. Requests and responses are screened by FACE’s guardrails like every other agent.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Automatic remediation is limited to the five actions above. It can never delete data, shut a host down or disable a security control (authentication, TLS or the circuit breaker itself). Every remediation is logged. Operators can turn automatic remediation off for the whole deployment, which narrows the agent to unhealthy-endpoint events. Everything else FACE recommends still waits for the named approver.
data.limitations#Limitations: It handles one event at a time and does not diagnose root causes across many services; a person does that from the notification and the log. A rollback reverts the most recent change that correlates with the fault, which is not always the cause.
data.model#Model: Runs on the deployment’s general model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen, Apache-2.0). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It receives one health event at a time and picks the single safest remediation from a fixed list:
Restart a runner or process that has stopped responding. Trip the circuit breaker to isolate a dependency that keeps failing. Roll back the most recent change that correlates with the fault. Scale to add capacity under sustained resource pressure. Notify a person when no safe automatic fix exists or the fault is ambiguous.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: One remediation from the list above, the target it applies to, a one-line rationale and a confidence between 0 and 1. A low-confidence or ambiguous case always becomes a notification for a person, not an action.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: A health event describing a degraded in-process resource (CPU, memory, goroutines, a panic) or an unreachable external endpoint.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: Inside your FACE deployment, on the deployment’s own inference. Health events stay in your deployment; no third-party AI service is involved.

data: Agent: the fulfilment agent (fulfilment in ExecuteLoop), working with FACE’s statistics engine.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Uses the reorder points and bounds you set. It never invents them. Refuses to force an order through or bypass a budget. Doesn’t favour suppliers on demographics, and doesn’t starve particular regions or groups of stock during a shortage. Refuses to reorder dispatch to favour anyone over your SLA commitments. Refuses to ignore temperature excursions or suppress cold-chain alerts to save cost or time.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A buyer approves every purchase order and expedite. The agent never places an order with a supplier on its own. Dispatch priorities and allocations it proposes are recommendations only.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl:
Invented data.
Records. SKU-31884: 1,800 on hand, 0 on order, 150 a day, lead time 14 days.
Draft. 12 days of cover (1,800 ÷ 150), less than the 14-day lead time, so a normal order arrives too late. About 300 units ((14 − 12) × 150) need expediting as premium freight. Purchase order drafted for the buyer’s approval.
data.limitations#Limitations: A forecast is not “exact stock needs”. It comes with its method and the history it had, so you can judge how far to trust it. With too little history, the statistics engine declines to forecast rather than guessing. It doesn’t allocate stock across a network of sites on its own judgement.
data.model#Model:
General reasoning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen, Apache-2.0). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
Forecasts come from FACE’s statistics engine, not from a language model. See Statistics & ML.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It reads stock, demand and lead times, says per item whether to do nothing, order now or expedite, and drafts the order for a buyer to approve. Its jobs:
Reorder decisions. Works out days of cover and states which of your reorder bounds was crossed, and by how much. Forecasts. Reads the statistics engine’s forecast, names the method that was used and how much history it had, and adjusts safety stock from it. Purchase orders. Drafts the order, with an expedite quantity and its premium freight cost kept separate from normal replenishment. Sourcing and service. Compares suppliers and carriers on the records you hold, measures on-time-in-full, and finds lanes worth consolidating. Dispatch documents. When an order is ready for dispatch, drafts the shipping documents (see Customs & trade documents).
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Action cards proposing a purchase order, an expedite or no action, each with the figures behind it. Operational procedures, ranked by the money and time they save.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Stock on hand and on order, demand history, lead times, reorder points and bounds, supplier and carrier records, order and delivery records, and the rules Rules Recon found in your data. It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane, on the customer’s Runink Server or in their cloud. No third-party AI service is called. See Facts shared by every card.

data: Agent: the voice dispatcher (voice), behind the phone line and the calling page.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: The phone line is the one path a person can reach without an account, so every utterance passes a length bound, the phrase filter and the voice guardrails before any model is called. A refusal is spoken to the caller. See AI safety. Gives no arrival time unless a planning speed is stated. Distances are labelled as straight-line estimates.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A dispatcher acts on every alert and every routing change. A call never changes routes or stops in your transport system.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl:
Invented data.
Driver. “Where’s my next drop and which door?”
Record. Stop 4 of 7: Granite Foods DC, door 12; note “call 10 minutes before arrival”. 14 km away in a straight line. No planning speed stated.
Reply. “Next drop is Granite Foods DC, door twelve. They ask for a call ten minutes before you arrive. It’s about fourteen kilometres in a straight line. I can’t give an arrival time without a planning speed.”
data.limitations#Limitations: It doesn’t give legal or medical advice to a driver in distress. It alerts a person. A transcript can mishear. Events it logs from speech are what the driver said, not vehicle telemetry. It doesn’t replace your telematics feed.
data.model#Model: Reasoning: general reasoning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen, Apache-2.0). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model. Speech recognition and speech synthesis run on services inside the deployment.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It lets a driver ask out loud where the next stop is, what the customer asked for or which door to use, and hear a short answer, with the call written to the log. Its jobs:
Answer the driver. Replies in a few spoken sentences from the dispatch record. Log what was said. Picks out the events a driver reports, such as speeding, a tyre-pressure warning, a long idle or an engine vibration, and writes them to the log. Alert a person. Raises anything urgent, such as a driver in distress, to a dispatcher.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A short spoken reply, synthesised as speech. Safety notifications and routing updates for a dispatcher. The telematics events the driver reported, for a dispatcher. The call itself is logged turn by turn; see Voice calls and the support log.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The transcript of what the driver said, the vehicle’s position, the stop list and customer notes on the dispatch record, and the rules Rules Recon found in your data. Its only tool is a read-only query.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane, on the customer’s Runink Server or in their cloud. No third-party AI service is called. A phone call is carried by your telephony provider, which carries the audio. On the calling page, call audio is transcribed as it arrives and then discarded, and the transcript is kept with the session. A caller’s words are never written to the process log.

data: Agents: the twins orchestrator (twins), the route twin (route_twin) and the common operational picture (cop), with the yard, border, custody and disruption cards.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Never makes up a distance or a time. A route the provider couldn’t compute is “unavailable”, never zero. A missing cause, capacity or cost figure is reported as missing. Doesn’t deprioritise neighbourhoods or regions on socioeconomic or demographic grounds, and doesn’t recommend hoarding capacity or price gouging. Refuses to de-anonymise people from aggregate trends, and refuses to fabricate sustainability figures.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A supervisor approves every action on a card, through TwinsService.ExecuteAction. Rejection needs a reason. The agents never dispatch a vehicle, book a carrier or send anything to a transport system on their own. Every action an orchestrator’s final answer proposes passes the judging ladder before it reaches the queue. An action the judge still disagrees with after one revision is removed.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl:
Invented data.
Records. Crossing at a land border: dwell 9.5 h against 3.0 h scheduled. Detention USD 90 per hour per load, 3 loads. Recorded cause: bill of lading number missing from the e-manifest.
Draft. Detention USD 2,565 (9.5 × 90 × 3). Priority Critical. Proposed for the supervisor’s approval: transmit corrected documents.
data.limitations#Limitations: An unrecorded handoff is not a break in custody. A ranked route is only as good as the provider’s answer and the criteria you named. An event flagged as single-source hasn’t been confirmed by a second source. It doesn’t establish who caused a delay beyond what the records state.
data.model#Model:
General reasoning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen, Apache-2.0). Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
Distances and travel times come from your routing provider, not from the model. The cards’ figures are fixed arithmetic over your records.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It reads yard snapshots, border and port events and transport records, flags the trailer, crossing or container that is costing money now, and drafts the action for the supervisor. Its jobs:
Yard capacity. Finds when the yard is over capacity and which arrivals were never recorded. Border waits. Works out detention from dwell time and the stated cost per hour, and proposes “transmit corrected documents” when the recorded cause is a document problem. Demurrage and detention. Separates days caused by documents from days caused by congestion. Service disruption. Records a disruption and its effect on open orders. Routes. Ranks the routes your routing provider returns on the criteria you name, with emissions per mode where a factor is stated. One picture. Ranks events from several sources by priority, life safety first, and flags events seen by only one source. Orchestration. The twins orchestrator maps each event to the right action card and hands work to the other agents on these cards.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Action cards in the Twins queue, each with a priority and one proposed action. See Action cards & money. Evidence documents such as CHAIN_OF_CUSTODY_AUDIT and SERVICE_DISRUPTION. A ranked list of routes and carriers, and a prioritised list of current events.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Yard snapshots and appointments, border crossing and port events, container free time and gate events, custody events, carrier and lane records, routes from your routing provider, sensor and camera findings, and the twin graph. It can run read-only queries against the connection a run was started with.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own model plane, on the customer’s Runink Server or in their cloud. No third-party AI service is called. See Facts shared by every card.

data:
This section is for the platform and SRE teams who deploy, configure, upgrade and troubleshoot a FACE instance. It is also for Runink operators. FACE runs on the Runink platform: Runink TIDE’s operators on a k0s cluster. FACE needs nothing outside that cluster to run. It calls no third-party model API and no managed cloud database, so the same procedures work air-gapped.
FACE is application code. TIDE provisions the cluster, runs the operators that build FACE’s pods, and serves the model plane FACE reasons with. The pages below say which side owns each setting, so you know whether to change a custom resource or the FACE image.
Deployment modelThe custom resources, the pods the operator builds, and what it injects into them. Prerequisites and orderingThe three secrets and one URL that must exist before the image runs, and the exact boot refusals. Configuration referenceEvery environment variable the code reads, grouped, with defaults. Model planeThe OpenAI-compatible contract, bringing a plane up, and the embedding dimension check. Persistence and backupMetaDB and Litestream, the appfs root, object and record stores, and custody of the key. RunnersOperating in-cluster fetch runners and self-hosted runners that enrol outbound. Upgrades and CDHow images are built and rolled, and what each upgrade leaves behind for a rollback. Local developmentcore dev up face, the release web build, and the smoke harness. Health and troubleshootingProbes, boot refusals, crashloops, empty panels, sign-in failures and embedding mismatch.
data.the-rule-behind-most-incidents#The rule: FACE refuses to start when a dependency it cannot work without is missing. It does not fall back to a degraded mode. This applies to the session signing key, the mesh CA, the at-rest key and the inference endpoint. A crashlooping pod with one clear log line is the intended result of a configuration fault. A pod that runs but serves nothing would be harder to diagnose. So read the first ❌ line of the container log before you look anywhere else. Health and troubleshooting lists each one.

data:
This reference was built from the code. It lists every environment variable read by the FACE backend (grpc/), the platform libraries it links (security, store, inference), its Litestream configuration and the frontend sleeve. It leaves out variables read only by build tooling, benchmarks and tests, and variables read only by the separate voice calling-agent image.
In a cluster, set values through the ControlPlane or FaceInstance env list, never on the live Deployment (see Deployment model). Locally, export them before core dev up face.
Secret in the Source column means the value is resolved through the platform secret backend (SECRET_BACKEND), so it can come from a mounted file instead of the environment. Everything else is read from the environment.
Connector and integration credentials (warehouses, SaaS APIs, maps keys) do not belong in environment variables. They are entered per connection in the cockpit and stored sealed in FACE’s credential store. The few integration variables below are the exceptions the code still reads.
data.authentication#Authentication: Variable Source Default Purpose ADMIN_EMAIL env none The break-glass admin account seeded at boot. ADMIN_PASSWORD secret none Its password. If either value is missing, FACE logs break-glass admin not seeded and disables password admin login. AUTH_GOOGLE_ONLY env unset true rejects password sign-in with Password sign-in is disabled — use Google sign-in. The break-glass admin is exempt. AUTH_SEED_USERS env none Comma-separated email=role pairs to seed. The operator projects them from ClientInstance users. AUTH_USERS_PATH env the data directory A legacy users file. It is imported once into the accounts table and then sealed as .migrated. OIDC_ISSUER env none The OIDC issuer. Single sign-on is on only when both this and OIDC_CLIENT_ID are set. OIDC_CLIENT_ID env none FACE’s OAuth client id, and the default token audience. It must equal the cockpit’s google_client_id. OIDC_AUDIENCE env OIDC_CLIENT_ID An explicit audience override. OIDC_JWKS_URL env discovered An explicit JWKS URL instead of discovery. AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS env none The single sign-on allowlist. When SSO is configured and this is empty, every SSO login is refused (SSO is not available on this instance). An unlisted account gets This account is not authorized for this instance. The operator projects it from the face-oauth Secret. Changes take effect when the pod restarts. FACE_RECAPTCHA_SITE_KEY env none The reCAPTCHA v3 site (public) key for login. The cockpit reads it from GET /auth/config. With no site key and no secret file on disk, logins are not captcha-checked, and the backend says so at boot. FACE_RECAPTCHA_SECRET_FILE secret path none Path to a file holding the reCAPTCHA secret key (a mounted Secret). It is read at each login, so a rotated Secret needs no restart. FACE_RECAPTCHA_HOSTNAMES env none Comma-separated FACE host(s) a token must have been minted on. Required once a key is present. With a key present but the configuration incomplete, every login is refused until it is complete. FACE_RECAPTCHA_MIN_SCORE env 0.5 The v3 score threshold, in [0,1].
data.connectors-vision-and-integrations#Conne: Variable Default Purpose FACE_BROWSER_CONCURRENCY 12 The number of headless-Chrome renders run at once. Lower it on small hosts. FACE_MAX_DOWNLOAD_BYTES 2 GiB The largest file a connector downloads. SCRAPER_USER_AGENT Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; RuninkFACE/1.0) The user agent for crawling. VISION_DETECT_INSTANCES off true adds a per-instance detection turn per camera frame. It roughly doubles the vision time per frame. VISION_MAX_EDGE 448 Frames are downscaled to this longest edge. 0 disables downscaling. Keep it below 1000. VISION_SWEEP_FRAMES 2 The number of frames sampled per camera ingest (at most 8). VISION_RESOLVE_ITEMS off true resolves detected objects against the item catalogue. OCR_VISION_FALLBACK off true lets OCR fall back to the vision model. GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS_JSON secret A Google Workspace service-account JSON. The stored integration config is used when it is empty. HUBSPOT_API_KEY none The key for the HubSpot read paths. TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID, TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN, TWILIO_FROM_NUMBER, TWILIO_WHATSAPP_FROM none Voice, SMS and WhatsApp. FACE refuses to send by name when they are missing. PUBLIC_URL localhost:8080 The public host used for Twilio media-stream callbacks. CALLING_AGENT_URL none The shared calling agent that WebRTC signalling is forwarded to. When it is unset, the call RPC answers Unavailable.
data.consensus-mesh-and-resilience#Consensus,: Variable Default Purpose RAFT_NODE_ID unset This node’s consensus id. When it is unset, the process does not join consensus (runners). When it is set, a failure to start the orchestrator stops the process. RAFT_PEERS none The peers, as id@host:port,…. RAFT_PIPE_DIR none The local proposal-pipe directory. RAFT_DATA_DIR unset (in memory) The durable consensus state. When it is unset, FACE warns that the state is memory-only. RAFT_MTLS_ADDR unset The listen address of the mTLS raft peer plane. A voting control plane must set it. RAFT_ADVERTISE_IP, RAFT_ADVERTISE_HOST none Extra IP and DNS SANs on the mesh leaf certificates. LOAD_SHED_THRESHOLD 0.85 The orchestrator’s load-shed threshold. SNAPSHOT_THRESHOLD, SNAPSHOT_RETAIN 1000, 100 Raft snapshot cadence and retention, in entries. WATCHDOG_CPU_THRESHOLD 99.5 The watchdog’s CPU alarm, in percent. WATCHDOG_MEMORY_THRESHOLD_MB library default The watchdog’s memory alarm. WATCHDOG_GOROUTINE_THRESHOLD 10000 The watchdog’s goroutine alarm. WATCHDOG_RUNNER_DIAL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 5 The runner reachability probe timeout. CIRCUIT_BREAKER_FAILURE_THRESHOLD 5 Failures before the breaker opens. CIRCUIT_BREAKER_RECOVERY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 30 How long the breaker stays open before it tries again. SELF_HEAL_AUTONOMOUS on false limits the self-healing reasoner to ENDPOINT_UNHEALTHY events.
data.embeddings#Embeddings: Variable Default Purpose EMBEDDING_URL INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL A dedicated embedding endpoint. Without it, embeddings go to the chat plane, and semantic grounding is expected to report INACTIVE. MODEL_EMBEDDING_DIM 768 The vector width the knowledge index is built for. The endpoint’s vectors must have this width after the format’s fit. EMBEDDING_FORMAT qwen3-embedding The instruction format of the embedding model: qwen3-embedding, nomic-v1.5 or raw. It must name the model EMBEDDING_URL actually serves. An unknown name stops the process. See Model plane.
data.fetch-runners-and-agents#Fetch, runners: Variable Default Purpose MANAGED_RUNNER_ENDPOINT face-runner:7102 Where the control plane forwards fetches. REQUIRE_RUNNER_ISOLATION unset true makes an unreachable runner a hard failure instead of a fallback to the control plane’s in-process SQL service. RUNNER_PORT none The port used when dialling a configured runner endpoint that has none. RUNNER_ENROLL_ADDR unset On a self-hosted runner, the control-plane address it enrols with (see Runners). RUNNER_ENROLL_TOKEN none The service-account token the runner enrols with. It is required when the address is set. RUNNER_ENROLL_TLS true TLS with system roots for the enrolment dial. RUNNER_NAME, RUNNER_VERSION empty Shown in the control plane’s runner registry. RUNNER_COMPUTE_POOL, RUNNER_CPU_LIMIT, RUNNER_MEMORY_LIMIT none, 1, 1G Inputs to runink runner create for the Snowflake runner type. FACE_RUNNER_CHANNEL_ADDR, FACE_RUNNER_CHANNEL_LISTEN none The address runners in Snowflake or Databricks reach FACE’s runner channel at, and the local listen address. Both must be set for those deploy targets to be offered. FACE_RUNNER_CA_DIR none The runner CA (ca.crt, ca.key), read by path. FACE_RUNNER_IMAGE_ARCHIVE, FACE_RUNNER_IMAGE_ARCHIVE_SHA256, FACE_RUNNER_IMAGE_REF, FACE_RUNNER_BINARY, FACE_RUNNER_BINARY_SHA256 none The runner artifacts an on-premises deploy copies, each with its SHA-256. FACE_RUNNER_GCP_IMAGE none The default digest-pinned runner image in your registry for a Google Cloud deploy. SCHEDULE_EXECUTE_FETCH off true makes schedules run real fetches. When it is off, a schedule logs a dry run. FETCH_CACHE_TTL 10m How long a fetch result may be reused. 0 disables reuse. FETCH_CACHE_MIN_CONFIDENCE 0.7 The minimum confidence for a cached result to be reused. FACE_RALPH_JUDGEMENT on off, false, 0, no or disabled turns off judging of proposed actions. FACE_RALPH_JUDGE_MAX_ACTIONS 3 The number of actions judged per answer (1–20). FACE_RALPH_JUDGE_REVISIONS 1 The number of revision rounds after dissent (0–3). FACE_FAST_JUDGEMENT on The local fast-path judge in front of the model. FACE_A2A_PEERS none Agent-to-agent delegation peers, separated by commas, spaces or newlines. A2A_ORGANIZATION falls back to RUNINK_ORG, then CORE_GITHUB_ORG The organization published on the agent card. FACE_AGENT_EMAIL_ALLOWLIST none The addresses or @domain suffixes the audit trail treats as approved recipients for agent e-mail. Agent e-mail is always drafted for a person to send, whatever this list or the decision-authority policy says. FACE_OUTPUT_URL_HOSTS none Hosts an agent answer may link to, comma separated; a subdomain matches its parent. Every other link is removed from the answer, and images and embedded frames are always removed. FACE_GUARD_MODEL none The model-router token of the guard tier (Qwen3Guard-Gen), usually guard. When set, the guard screens untrusted input and agent answers in the agent loop; an agent whose proposals reach an approver refuses the run when the guard flags a jailbreak or cannot assess the text. FACE_PROMPT_GUARD on Set to off to stop the guard model even when FACE_GUARD_MODEL is set. The OpenBias rules and the output constraints are never switched off. FACE_AUTHORITY_POLICY_FILE embedded default A decision-authority policy (versioned JSON) replacing the shipped one. Unreadable or invalid = every approval refused. ENFORCE_AUDIT_LOGGING, REQUIRE_HITL, DATABASE_ENGINE, PRIMARY_SERVER_URL unset Reported into every compliance analysis as the controls actually in place. They never stop the process.
data.frontend-sleeve#Frontend sleeve: PORT (default 8080), WEB_DIR (/web) and BACKEND_ADDR. See Deployment model.
data.inference-and-the-model-plane#Inference: Variable Default Purpose INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL none (required) The base URL for chat completions, and for embeddings when EMBEDDING_URL is unset. INFERENCE_API_KEY empty Secret. Sent as Authorization: Bearer when it is set. FACE never generates one. The placeholder application-generated-key counts as empty. VISION_REMOTE_URL INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL The base URL for vision calls. VOICE_REMOTE_URL INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL The base URL for voice calls. INFERENCE_CONTEXT_SIZE 16384 The prompt window, in tokens, that the agent loop budgets against. INFERENCE_DECODE_TOK_S 3.4 The measured decode rate of the text tier. It sizes time budgets. INFERENCE_VISION_DECODE_TOK_S 1.0 The same, for the vision tier. REACT_DECODE_TOK_S INFERENCE_DECODE_TOK_S Overrides the decode rate for the agent loop’s turn budgets. REACT_PREFILL_TOK_S 38 The prefill rate for the agent loop’s turn budgets. POSTURE_DECODE_TOK_S INFERENCE_DECODE_TOK_S Overrides the decode rate for posture analysis. POSTURE_LLM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 120 The model time budget for posture analysis. COMPLIANCE_LLM_BUDGET_SECONDS 15 The model time budget for compliance analysis. METASEARCH_BUDGET_SECONDS 90 The time budget for the trend metasearch step of a fetch. FACE_ADMIT_MAX 0 (off) The maximum number of concurrent inference calls. 0 dispatches directly with no scheduling. The operator sets 1. FACE_ADMIT_QUEUE 0 (unbounded) The maximum number of waiters before backpressure. The operator sets 32. FACE_ADMIT_MODE reject reject or degrade when the queue is full. FACE_ADMIT_WEIGHTS none Tier weights, for example interactive:4,batch:1. FACE_ADMIT_COALESCE off true lets identical concurrent prompts share one generation. FACE_GATE_MAX_INFLIGHT off The concurrent-submission cap of the inference gate. FACE_GATE_FIRST_TOKEN_SECONDS off The longest acceptable queue wait. The gate is on only when this or FACE_GATE_MAX_INFLIGHT is positive. FACE_GATE_DECODE_RATE none The measured tokens per second the gate assumes. FACE_GATE_REQUEST_SECONDS off The per-request time budget for inference calls. These variables are read into the process configuration for compatibility. FACE starts no model server of its own, so they neither choose nor tune what the plane serves. Set the model on the plane instead. They are: INFERENCE_PORT, INFERENCE_HOST, INFERENCE_MODEL, INFERENCE_TIMEOUT, INFERENCE_PARALLEL, INFERENCE_CACHE_RAM, INFERENCE_CPU_STRICT, INFERENCE_THREADS, INFERENCE_BATCH, INFERENCE_GPU_LAYERS, INTERNAL_INFERENCE_IP, INTERNAL_BRIDGE_IP, INTERNAL_SUBNET, MODEL_DIR, MODEL_EMBEDDING, MODEL_VOXTRAL, MODEL_WHISPER, MODEL_INFERENCE_TTS, MODEL_WAV_TOKENIZER and MODEL_VISION. (MODEL_VISION is also printed in the boot line that names the vision tier.)
data.process-role-and-platform#Process, role: Variable Default Purpose SERVICE_ROLE control plane runner makes this process a fetch runner. Any other value makes it a control plane. The operator sets server or runner. PORT none The default for serve --port. The image entrypoint uses 7000 when PORT is unset. The operator sets 7100 (control plane) or 7102 (runner). APP_VERSION empty The version stamped on structured logs. SECRET_BACKEND env env or file. With file, secrets are read from SECRETS_DIR with the environment as fallback. Any other value makes every secret lookup fail. SECRETS_DIR /var/run/secrets The directory for the file backend. A file is named after the variable, or in lower case with dashes. RUNINK_VARIANT standard The declared variant. demo seeds the demo connection set. When the process has no in-cluster ServiceAccount token, demo also offers a single local-development instance in the instance picker. DEMO_SEED_DATA unset true also seeds the demo connection set. It does not enable the local instance card. Prefer RUNINK_VARIANT=demo. RUNINK_APP face The app name that filters ClientInstances in the instance picker. FACE_CLIENT_INSTANCE none The name of this deployment’s own ClientInstance, used by the access page. There is no fallback. FACE_CLIENT_INSTANCE_NAMESPACE POD_NAMESPACE The namespace of that ClientInstance. POD_NAMESPACE none The pod’s namespace, from the downward API. Also used when publishing connectors to Runink TIDE. POD_NAME none The instance name on lineage reports sent to TIDE. HOSTNAME set by Kubernetes The runner id fallback when RUNNER_ID is unset. KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST, KUBERNETES_SERVICE_PORT kubernetes.default.svc, 443 The API server FACE lists ClientInstances from. TENANT_ID none The pod’s tenant for subscription checks. Also names the connectors ConfigMap FACE publishes to TIDE (face-). SUBSCRIPTION_TIER, SUBSCRIPTION_STATUS, SUBSCRIPTION_SEATS none The subscription the operator mirrors from the ClientInstance. A subscription is reported only when the tier and TENANT_ID are set and match the tenant asked about. RUNINK_ACCOUNTS_FILE none The account file the platform operator provides, mapping each user to the purchaser whose billing account pays for their model time. Unset, every model call is recorded as unattributed and logged, never billed to another account. See Plans and billing. CORE_ROUTER_BILLING_KEY_FILE, CORE_ROUTER_BILLING_KID none The key file (read by path) and key id FACE signs each model call’s billing claim with. Unset, model calls carry no billing claim. It never blocks or fails a call. CORE_PLATFORM_ADMIN none The installation admin’s e-mail. That account sees every instance. When it is unset, nobody gets that grant. LICENSE none A signed licence blob, as base64 or raw JSON. LICENSE_FILE none A path to read the licence from when LICENSE is unset. LICENSE_PUBLIC_KEY none The base64 Ed25519 public key licences are verified against. FACE_MODEL_CAP_FETCH_PER_HOUR, FACE_MODEL_CAP_ASK_PER_HOUR, FACE_MODEL_CAP_LOOP_PER_HOUR, FACE_MODEL_CAP_SIMULATE_PER_HOUR, FACE_MODEL_CAP_VISION_PER_HOUR 60, 120, 30, 60, 240 How many model-backed runs one user may start per hour, per class: fetches (RunFetch, RunFetchStream), QuickAsk, agent loops (ExecuteLoop), simulations (SimulateScenario, InteractiveSimulate) and vision (ExtractText, IngestSurveillanceFeed). A call over the cap gets RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED with the time until the next slot. 0 turns that class’s cap off. Counted per process. CORE_HEALTH_URL, CORE_HEALTH_TOKEN none Where FACE reports observed lineage to the TIDE console, and the bearer token it uses. CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS unset A comma-separated allowlist of browser origins for gRPC-web. Set it to your cockpit origin(s). FACE_RATE_RPS, FACE_RATE_BURST 10, 60 The per-user request rate (requests per second, sustained) and burst. Each is defaulted on its own. Requests are counted per signed-in user, across all of that user’s sessions and tabs; requests without a valid session are counted per client address. A unary call and a stream open each count as one request. Callers over the limit get RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED. FACE_RATE_RPS=0 turns the limit off. A value that does not parse keeps the default. ENV, GCP_REGION empty Labels printed into the system state that compliance and domain analyses read.
data.removed-and-renamed-names#Removed and re:
These are listed to help an upgrade. FACE ignores every one of them, except OBJECTSTORE_USE_SSL, which it refuses. Remove them from your resources.
Name Status REMOTE_LLAMA_URL, LLAMA_REMOTE_URL Renamed to INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL. A manifest that sets only the old name has no inference endpoint, and the process refuses to start. LLAMA_API_KEY Renamed to INFERENCE_API_KEY. MESH_MTLS, ENABLE_ALTS Removed. Mesh mTLS is unconditional. REQUIRE_MTLS_INGRESS Removed. OBJECTSTORE_USE_SSL Removed, and refused if it is set. Put the scheme in OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT. CORE_ENVELOPE_ENCRYPTION Removed. Sealing at rest is unconditional. GOOGLE_API_KEY Read by no code. Maps keys are entered per connection in the cockpit.
data.required-at-boot#Required at boot: Variable Source Purpose AUTH_JWT_SECRET secret Signs the pre-TOTP MFA challenge. The process refuses to start without it. MESH_CA_CERT secret The shared cluster CA certificate. Each pod issues its own rotating mTLS leaves from it. MESH_CA_KEY secret The shared cluster CA private key. CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK secret A base64-encoded 32-byte key-encryption key for everything sealed at rest. INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL env The base URL of the shared inference plane. No other name is read for it. Prerequisites and ordering has the exact refusal messages.
data.storage-and-persistence#Storage and pers: Variable Source Default Purpose OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT env unset The object store (host:port or https://host:port). When it is unset, the appfs root uses an encrypted local directory. A cleartext endpoint is accepted only for a loopback or cluster-internal name. OBJECTSTORE_ACCESS_KEY, OBJECTSTORE_SECRET_KEY secret none Object-store credentials. They are required when an endpoint is set. OBJECTSTORE_VACUUM_ACCESS_KEY, OBJECTSTORE_VACUUM_SECRET_KEY secret none An optional second credential used for every delete. Set both or neither. OBJECTSTORE_BUCKET env core The object-store bucket for records, knowledge and evidence. The appfs root always uses its own bucket, face. CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK_RETIRED secret none Retired KEKs (comma- or space-separated, base64), accepted for decryption only. SQLITE_PATH /face.db The MetaDB file. The entrypoint requires an absolute path. The operator sets /data/face.db. FACE_APPFS_DIR appfs/ beside face.db The encrypted local appfs root, used only when there is no object store. FACE_UPLOAD_DIR uploads/ beside face.db The instance’s private upload directory, created mode 0700. An OCR LOCAL source and a fetch attachment named by file name are read only from here, and uploaded attachments are written here. It may not be /tmp or another shared system directory, and there is no temp-directory fallback. FACE_CCTV_CAPTURE_DIRS none Extra absolute directories (colon-separated) in which a camera connection may name a local video file. The upload directory is always included. Any other local path is refused. FACE_TENANT default-tenant The tenant sub-root, tenants//. Set it before the first boot (see Persistence). RUNNER_ID HOSTNAME On a runner, names its private tables. The operator sets a stable value. FACE_CONNECTIONS_DIR none The legacy connection directory. It is imported once into the appfs root. FACE_DCI_CORPUS_DIR none Overrides the directory the grep-based grounding reads. FETCH_LEDGER_DIR ./data/fetch-ledger The fetch cascade ledger. RALPH_RUN_DIR ./data/ralph-runs The agent run journal, used to resume runs. FACE_VOICE_SOURCE_DIR $RALPH_RUN_DIR/voice-sources Where recorded voice sources are written. RALPH_READ_ROOT . The root agents may read files under. Paths that escape it are rejected. FEATURED_MESSAGES_PATH featured_messages.json on the data path A file of featured activity messages. FACE_DEPLOY_SECRETS_DIR none A directory of runner deploy secrets, read by path. EVIDENCE_FRAME_RETENTION 0 (none kept) How long camera evidence frames are kept, as a Go duration. It is capped at 720h. Litestream, read by /app/litestream.yml and set by the operator: SQLITE_PATH, MINIO_ENDPOINT (host and port only, with no scheme), MINIO_BUCKET, MINIO_ACCESS_KEY, MINIO_SECRET_KEY. The image entrypoint also checks MINIO_ENDPOINT to decide whether to run the server under Litestream.

data:
A FACE instance has three workloads. The operators in Runink TIDE build most of them. The image is the same for the control plane and the runners. Only the role differs.
Workload Role Built by Container port Control plane SERVICE_ROLE=server. It serves the cockpit’s gRPC-web and gRPC API, holds sessions and metadata, runs schedules and self-healing, and forwards every fetch to a runner. It never runs a fetch itself. runink operator, from a ControlPlane resource 7100 Fetch runner SERVICE_ROLE=runner. It runs the fetch pipeline (connectors, derivations, agents) on dedicated compute. runink operator, from a FaceInstance resource, or a static manifest (see below) 7102 Frontend sleeve It serves the Flutter web bundle with a single-page-app fallback and reverse-proxies backend calls to the control plane. Static manifest in TIDE’s on-host bundle 8080 in the image TLS for browsers ends at the platform edge in front of these workloads. FACE itself is not configured with a certificate for the browser.
data.the-custom-resources#The custom resource:
The runink operator (in TIDE, grpc/operators/runink) owns two kinds in the API group runink.org/v1alpha1.
ControlPlane (short name cp) describes the control plane.
Field Effect image The FACE backend image. replicas The pod count. The Deployment uses the Recreate strategy (see Upgrades). raftNodeId This control plane’s consensus node id, by convention 1. tenant Becomes FACE_TENANT. When it is empty, the operator uses the one tenant that all of this control plane’s FaceInstances name. If they name more than one, FACE_TENANT is left unset and the operator logs that. objectStoreEndpoint The object-store Service, as host:port with no scheme. It is used for OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT and for Litestream. The default is face-objectd:9000. embeddingUrl Becomes EMBEDDING_URL. managedRunnerEndpoint Becomes MANAGED_RUNNER_ENDPOINT: the host:port the control plane forwards fetches to. scheduleExecuteFetch Sets SCHEDULE_EXECUTE_FETCH=true. ambassador Adds the optional mTLS ambassador sidecar. probes Tunes the kubelet probes (see Health and troubleshooting). env Extra environment variables. They are appended after the operator’s own list, so a literal here overrides the operator’s value of the same name. FACE_TENANT, RUNNER_ID and the default FACE_APPFS_DIR are appended after env, so you cannot override those three with env. nodeSelector A hard pin to labelled nodes, on top of the operator’s default placement. FaceInstance (short name fi) describes one tenant’s fetch runner. The operator names the runner Deployment face-runner-.
Field Effect tenant The tenant this runner serves. It becomes FACE_TENANT. It must equal the control plane’s tenant, because the control plane reads the fetch results this runner writes under that tenant. image The FACE backend image. controlPlaneRef The ControlPlane whose mesh this runner joins. computeUnits The tenant’s compute budget. The operator turns it into CPU and memory requests and limits and reports them in status.allocatedCpu and status.allocatedMemory. tier managed (the default) or local. gpu Requests GPU scheduling. embeddingUrl Becomes EMBEDDING_URL on the runner. inference.model The model hint for the runner. The other inference.* fields (gpuLayers, contextSize, parallel, threads, batch) are deprecated. They are still accepted so that existing resources validate, but the operator no longer writes them anywhere. suspend Scales the runner to zero without deleting the resource. env, nodeSelector, probes, ambassador As on ControlPlane. status.phase moves through Pending, Provisioning, Ready, Degraded and Suspended.
A third kind, ClientInstance (core.runink.org/v1alpha1), is owned by TIDE’s core operator. It records an instance’s app, tenant, image, users and subscription. FACE reads it in two ways:
The cockpit’s instance picker lists ClientInstances whose spec.app matches RUNINK_APP (default face). The pod’s ServiceAccount needs list on clientinstances.core.runink.org for this. The operator mirrors a ClientInstance’s users and subscription onto the pod as AUTH_SEED_USERS, SUBSCRIPTION_TIER, SUBSCRIPTION_STATUS, SUBSCRIPTION_SEATS and TENANT_ID. The operator is the source of truth for the pod spec. If you edit a running Deployment, the operator reconciles your change away. Change the ControlPlane or FaceInstance resource instead, usually through its env list.
data.the-frontend-sleeve#The frontend sleeve:
The sleeve (flutter/sleeve/) is a small static Go server in a distroless image. It serves /web and forwards a request to BACKEND_ADDR when the request is one of these:
a gRPC-web request; a request under /auth/, /api/ or /webrtc/; a dotted gRPC service path. The release web build bakes in no backend host. The cockpit takes its origin from the page it was loaded from, so one bundle works behind any hostname.
Variable Default Purpose PORT 8080 The listen port. WEB_DIR /web The Flutter bundle directory. BACKEND_ADDR the control-plane Service Where backend calls are forwarded. The edge may split gRPC-web off to the control plane before a request reaches the sleeve. In that case the sleeve only serves the static bundle.
data.the-static-on-host-manifests#The static:
TIDE’s on-host bundle (grpc/infrastructure/apps/onhost/40-face.yaml, applied with kubectl apply -k infrastructure/apps/onhost from TIDE’s grpc/ directory) declares two FACE workloads that no operator reconciles:
face-frontend, the sleeve. BACKEND_ADDR points it at the control-plane Service. face-runner, a static fetch runner (SERVICE_ROLE=runner, port 7102). The backend’s default MANAGED_RUNNER_ENDPOINT is face-runner:7102, and it points at this runner. The control plane is not in that file. The runink operator owns it, so edit the ControlPlane resource and not the manifest.
data.what-the-operator-puts-in-the-control-pl:
Containers
face-backend runs /app/server serve --port 7100. litestream runs litestream replicate -config /app/litestream.yml. It continuously replicates the SQLite metadata database. The ambassador sidecar is added when spec.ambassador enables it. Init containers, in this order:
Two ownership init containers prepare the connections volume and the raft volume. The connections directory is made owner-only (mode 0700). ensure-bucket runs /app/server ensure-bucket. litestream-restore runs litestream restore -if-db-not-exists -if-replica-exists -config /app/litestream.yml /data/face.db. Volumes
Mount Kind Holds /data emptyDir face.db (SQLITE_PATH=/data/face.db). It is rebuilt from the Litestream replica on every pod start. /raft node-local hostPath, one per member Consensus state (RAFT_DATA_DIR). /connections node-local hostPath, one per member The legacy connection layout (FACE_CONNECTIONS_DIR). When no object store is configured, it also holds the encrypted appfs root at /connections/appfs. Environment. The operator sets the role, port, raft settings, inference and embedding URLs, object-store and Litestream settings, and admission defaults (FACE_ADMIT_MAX=1, FACE_ADMIT_QUEUE=32). It also references these Secrets:
Secret Keys Required on the pod Created by the operator face-session AUTH_JWT_SECRET yes yes, if it is absent. It is never rotated on reconcile. core-envelope-kek CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK yes yes, if it is absent. It is never overwritten. core-mesh-ca MESH_CA_CERT, MESH_CA_KEY yes no. You distribute it with core mesh ca --namespace . -admin email, password yes yes. It holds the break-glass admin as ADMIN_EMAIL and ADMIN_PASSWORD. objectd-key-face-app, objectd-key-face-litestream, objectd-key-face-vacuum access-key, secret-key yes, once they exist by TIDE’s provisioner. Until they exist, the pod keeps the shared objectstore-creds pair. face-oauth google-client-id, allowed-emails optional no license LICENSE, LICENSE_PUBLIC_KEY optional no. You mint it with TIDE’s license tool. A required reference to a missing Secret stops the pod before FACE runs. Kubernetes reports it as CreateContainerConfigError and names the Secret. That is deliberate: the cause shows up in kubectl describe pod and does not have to be found in an application log.
The runner pod is built the same way. The differences: it runs as SERVICE_ROLE=runner on port 7102, and RUNNER_ID is the runner Deployment’s name, so the runner’s own state survives restarts. It does not set RAFT_NODE_ID, because runners are not consensus voters.

data: This page is for Runink operators and contributors who have the FACE source and its sibling repositories checked out side by side. The FACE repository does not stand up a stack by itself. Runink TIDE’s core CLI owns the development stack (the tide CLI; core still works as an alias).
data.build-and-serve-the-cockpit-release#Buil:
core dev up runs the Flutter app in debug mode, which often never paints. For anything you intend to look at, build the release bundle and point it at the local backend:
cd flutter flutter build web --release --no-tree-shake-icons \ --dart-define=BACKEND_URL=http://127.0.0.1:$PORT \ --dart-define=SERVER_HOST=127.0.0.1 \ --dart-define=SERVER_PORT=$PORT \ --dart-define=WEB_PORT=$PORT \ --dart-define=SERVER_SECURE=false \ --dart-define=DEBUG_AUTO_LOGIN=false cd .. go run .claude/skills/run-face/smoke.go serve flutter/build/web 3001 & These --dart-define values are for local use only. The production image bakes in no backend host: the cockpit uses the origin it was loaded from.
data.export-the-backends-configuration#Export:
core dev up passes its environment through to the backend, and it creates the mesh CA and the envelope KEK as dev files. You supply everything else:
export FACE_REPO=/path/to/face # the checkout to build; --face-repo alone is not enough export ADMIN_EMAIL='devadmin@localhost.test' export ADMIN_PASSWORD='' export AUTH_JWT_SECRET='' # required: the backend exits without it export RUNINK_VARIANT=demo # local instance card + demo connections export INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL='http://127.0.0.1:' # required export EMBEDDING_URL='http://127.0.0.1:' export MODEL_EMBEDDING_DIM=768 Bring up an OpenAI-compatible model server first, as described in Model plane. A dead loopback port is enough for the process to boot, but then it has no model.
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites:
Go 1.26, buf, grpcurl, Flutter and a Chrome or Chromium browser.
The sibling repositories next to face/: core, inference, mesh, security, store, ml, web, ui and billing. The Go build resolves them through relative replace directives.
The generated protobuf code. It is not committed, so generate it first:
cd grpc && buf generate && cd .. cd grpc && go build ./... && cd ..
data.start-it#Start it:
./core dev up face --face-repo "$FACE_REPO" > /tmp/face-devup.log 2>&1 & until grep -qE 'backend ready on ephemeral|❌' /tmp/face-devup.log; do sleep 5; done PORT=$(grep -oE 'ephemeral gRPC port [0-9]+' /tmp/face-devup.log | grep -oE '[0-9]+$') The backend’s gRPC port is chosen fresh on every start. Read it from the log line ✅ [face] backend ready on ephemeral gRPC port . core dev up face also starts a second FACE process with SERVICE_ROLE=runner, and points the control plane at it, so fetches work.
If you run the two processes by hand instead, start the runner with SERVICE_ROLE=runner, and give the control plane MANAGED_RUNNER_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:. If the two processes use separate data directories, they must still share one FACE_APPFS_DIR. Sessions live in the appfs root, so a runner with its own root rejects every forwarded fetch with invalid or expired session token. AUTH_JWT_SECRET and ADMIN_PASSWORD can come from owner-only files instead of the environment (SECRET_BACKEND=file SECRETS_DIR=).
data.the-smoke-harnesses#The smoke harnesses:
Both harnesses are single-file Go programs using only the standard library, run from the repository root. Build them before use. go run turns every non-zero exit code into 1, and here the exit code is the result.
smoke.go signs in through the real cockpit over the Chrome DevTools Protocol, picks the instance, and screenshots the Fetch, AI Center, Rules, Lab, Twins and Schedules pages:
go build -o /tmp/face-smoke .claude/skills/run-face/smoke.go /tmp/face-smoke "$ADMIN_EMAIL" "$ADMIN_PASSWORD" /tmp/face-shots; echo "exit=$?" Exit 1 means the login never left the login route. Exit 2 means it logged in, but a route bounced back to the login page, so the screenshot shows the login card. Look at the PNGs: a blank white image means the Flutter engine never painted.
simulate-smoke.go proves the backend returns real data. It signs in, checks that the inference plane answers, lists the scenarios, runs one simulation, and turns the result into an exit code:
go build -o /tmp/simulate-smoke .claude/skills/run-face/simulate-smoke.go /tmp/simulate-smoke "$PORT"; echo "exit=$?" Exit Meaning 0 Populated: traces, impacts and scenarios came back. 1 It could not complete: an unexpected RPC error, or the time budget (--timeout, default 10m) ran out. 2 A precondition failed, and the message names it: nothing listening, login refused, inference plane unreachable, or no scenarios yet (which needs a completed fetch or a demo instance). 3 The call ran, but every payload field is empty. 4 TOON_PARSE_FAILURE: the model’s reply did not match the template’s contract. Minutes per simulation are normal on CPU-only inference.

data: All of FACE’s reasoning runs on a model plane inside your cluster: text generation, embeddings, vision grading, and every agent (rules, posture, twins, compliance, the fetch cascade). FACE is an HTTP client of that plane. It ships no inference binary, starts no model process and has no local fallback. Runink TIDE runs the plane. mistral.rs is the intended engine, but nothing in FACE’s client is specific to mistral.rs.
data.check-the-boot-log#Check the boot log:
A healthy start logs:
🧭 Routing reasoning to the shared inference plane at (no local model server) 🧭 Embedding: tier , vector space About 15 seconds later, and after up to 12 retries while the model loads, one grounding line follows (see below).
data.prove-the-plane-answers-through-face#Pro:
The boot check only proves that a URL is set. To prove that a model answers, sign in and call ModelService/Generate through FACE itself:
TOK=$(grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"method":"AUTH_METHOD_CREDENTIALS","username":"'"$ADMIN_EMAIL"'","password":"'"$ADMIN_PASSWORD"'"}' \ 127.0.0.1:$PORT semantics.v1.IdentityService/Login | grep -o '"token": "[^"]*"' | cut -d'"' -f4) test -n "$TOK" || echo "LOGIN RETURNED NO TOKEN" grpcurl -plaintext -H "authorization: Bearer $TOK" \ -d '{"prompt":"Say hello in one sentence.","temperature":0,"max_tokens":40}' \ 127.0.0.1:$PORT semantics.v1.ModelService/Generate A reply with model text and "finishReason": "stop" means the whole path works. In a cluster, run this against a kubectl port-forward to the pod’s app port. The login field is token. If that field comes back empty, the next call fails with invalid or expired session token, and the error points at the wrong call.
data.set-the-endpoint-variables#Set the endpo: export INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL='http://127.0.0.1:' export EMBEDDING_URL='http://127.0.0.1:' export MODEL_EMBEDDING_DIM=768 export EMBEDDING_FORMAT= In a cluster, set the same names in the resource’s env. The operator already sets them for the ControlPlane and FaceInstance pods.
data.start-an-openai-compatible-server#Start: In a cluster, TIDE’s inference manifests provide the plane. Use the Service URL TIDE gives you. For a local run, any OpenAI-compatible server works. Serve a chat model on one port and an embedding model on another, because a chat model answering /v1/embeddings returns unusable vectors.
data.the-contract#The contract:
The plane must speak the OpenAI-compatible HTTP API:
Call Request Notes Chat POST /v1/chat/completions Always sent with "stream": true. FACE reads server-sent events. Embeddings POST /v1/embeddings One input string per request. Auth Authorization: Bearer Sent only when INFERENCE_API_KEY is non-empty. The model field carries a task id, not a file name: default for general reasoning, coder for code tasks and vision for vision tasks. Embedding requests send default. A router in front of the engines can use this id to send each task to the right tier. Vision and voice calls go to VISION_REMOTE_URL and VOICE_REMOTE_URL. Both default to INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL.
data.the-embedding-dimension-check#The embedd:
The knowledge index is built for vectors of width MODEL_EMBEDDING_DIM (default 768). EMBEDDING_FORMAT says how to wrap queries and documents for the embedding model, and how to fit its output to that width. The default, qwen3-embedding, cuts a 1024-dimension vector to 768. At boot, FACE embeds one probe string and logs exactly one of these lines:
✅ Comet grounding ACTIVE: embedding endpoint returns 768-dim vectors in space ⚠️ Comet grounding INACTIVE: the embedding tier did not answer after warmup () — grounding falls back to DCI grep ⚠️ Comet grounding INACTIVE: the embedding endpoint returned an empty or all-zero vector (a chat model answering /v1/embeddings does this) — grounding falls back to DCI grep ⚠️ Comet grounding INACTIVE: embedding endpoint returns -dim vectors, index expects (MODEL_EMBEDDING_DIM), and the format cannot fit them — grounding falls back to DCI grep When EMBEDDING_URL is unset, the tier line says so, and INACTIVE is expected:
🧭 Embedding: no dedicated embedding tier (EMBEDDING_URL unset): embeddings go to the chat plane, which serves no embedding model, so semantic grounding is expected to be INACTIVE; vector space INACTIVE does not stop the process. Search falls back to keyword grep over the document corpus, so answers still come back, but with weaker grounding. Fix it by pointing EMBEDDING_URL at a real embedding model, and by setting MODEL_EMBEDDING_DIM and EMBEDDING_FORMAT to match that model.
ACTIVE proves only the width of the vectors. A different model that returns the same width looks identical from FACE. Each format and width gets its own knowledge index (knowledge--d; raw keeps the original knowledge index). Changing EMBEDDING_FORMAT therefore starts an empty index and leaves the old one untouched as a rollback. FACE does not re-embed existing documents at boot.
data.what-each-failure-looks-like#What each f: Situation What you see INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL unset The process exits at boot with no inference endpoint configured: INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL is unset or blank. An endpoint was never configured for one call path That RPC fails with FailedPrecondition: is unavailable: no inference endpoint configured (INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL is unset or blank)… The plane requires a token and INFERENCE_API_KEY is empty An HTTP 401 on each call. It is not a boot failure. The plane is reachable but the model is still loading, or the model id is not served A per-call error from the plane. The boot check does not catch it.

data:
FACE keeps its state on self-hosted storage inside your cluster. There is no managed cloud database. Every store below is sealed at rest under keys derived from one platform key-encryption key, CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK. That makes the KEK the most important thing to back up (see Key custody).
Store What it holds Where it lives appfs root Sessions, accounts, connections and their credentials, application metadata, fetch results, schedules, rule policies, compute budgets The object-store bucket face, or an encrypted local directory MetaDB (face.db) A small SQLite key-value store on the control plane SQLITE_PATH, replicated by Litestream Record store Session traces (with embedding vectors) and feedback, as self-describing Avro The object store Knowledge corpus One semantic index per tenant: a write-ahead log plus sealed snapshots The object store, under comet//knowledge/, or /knowledge/ Camera evidence Evidence frames, when EVIDENCE_FRAME_RETENTION is set The object store Fetch ledger The fetch cascade’s ledger FETCH_LEDGER_DIR on local disk
data.credential-store#Credential store:
A connection’s credentials never sit in an environment variable or in the connection record. The connection record has no field a secret would fit in. When a connection is saved, secret-named fields are lifted into a credential bundle. Bundles are stored as rows of the tenant table tenants//var/lib/connections (credentials/), sealed under FACE’s derived key and bound to their path. Consensus replicates only the connection metadata snapshot, never the credentials.
Where FACE writes to local disk (the local appfs root, the knowledge corpus without an object store), directories are created 0700 and files 0600. The older layout (FACE_CONNECTIONS_DIR, with connections.json and credentials/*.json) is imported once on a persistent root, and each imported file is renamed .migrated.
data.key-custody#Key custody:
CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK is a base64-encoded 32-byte key held in the core-envelope-kek Secret. The runink operator creates it if it is absent, and never rotates or overwrites it.
Losing the KEK loses the data. The MetaDB values, the whole appfs root (sessions, accounts, connection credentials, metadata), the sealed object-store objects and the knowledge snapshots cannot be decrypted without it. No recovery path exists, by design. Export the Secret to your offline key escrow as soon as it is created. Back it up separately from the data it protects. To change keys, keep the old key readable. CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK_RETIRED takes a list of earlier KEKs (base64, separated by commas or whitespace). FACE and the storage libraries use them for decryption only, and seal new writes under CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK. If you replace the KEK without listing the old one as retired, everything sealed under the old key becomes unreadable.
data.metadb-and-litestream#MetaDB and Litestr:
The control plane keeps a SQLite database, face.db, at SQLITE_PATH. It seals every value before the value is written, so both the local file and its replica hold ciphertext. Keys are not sealed, because the store does prefix scans on them. Never put secret material in a key. Runners open no SQLite database.
The image bundles Litestream 0.5.17, pinned by SHA-256, and the configuration /app/litestream.yml:
Setting Value Replica S3-compatible, path-style, litestream/face.db in MINIO_BUCKET at MINIO_ENDPOINT Sync interval 1 second Compaction levels 2 minutes, 10 minutes, 1 hour Snapshots every hour, kept for 24 hours The /data volume is an emptyDir. On every pod start, the operator’s litestream-restore init container rebuilds face.db from the replica when a replica exists and no local file does. After that, the litestream sidecar replicates continuously. When the image runs on its own (outside the operator), its entrypoint does the same when MINIO_ENDPOINT is set:
litestream: restoring /app/grpc/data/face.db from MinIO (if a replica exists)... litestream: replicating /app/grpc/data/face.db -> MinIO; launching server... If MINIO_ENDPOINT is unset, it prints Litestream/MinIO not configured — running server without WAL replication. A failed restore stops the container with litestream restore failed: .
data.migrations-leave-a-rollback-in-place#Mig:
Each move to a new storage layout copies the data once and leaves the old copy behind, so you can go back to an older image:
Legacy metadata files are imported once into their table. Each one is then replaced by an envelope-sealed .migrated. To read one back:
go run -C grpc ./cmd/faceops metalog-unseal --table .migrated Older object-store tables (tables/face// in the object store’s own bucket) are copied into the appfs root on first open, and only into a table that has never been written. The originals are left in place.
The old knowledge index (comet/index.gob) is migrated once. The marker is face/migrations/comet-index-gob.v1.json. After that the gob is never written again, so an older image still boots, minus anything indexed after the switch.
data.the-appfs-root#The appfs root:
At boot, FACE mounts its own application root, and it will not serve without it. When OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT is set, the root is the bucket face on the object store. Otherwise, it is an encrypted local directory, FACE_APPFS_DIR. The root’s key is derived from the KEK for FACE alone, and every block is bound to its full path, so a sealed block cannot be moved to another path and still open. The boot log says which backend is in use:
🗂️ FACE appfs root online: objectstore bucket face, tenant 🗂️ FACE appfs root online: encrypted local directory /face, tenant The root is split into two scopes:
Deployment-wide: sessions (run/sessions), accounts (var/lib/auth_users) and compute budgets. Per tenant (tenants//, default default-tenant): connections and their credentials, application metadata, the four fetch snapshots, schedules, remediation overlays and routes, rule policies and support calls. A runner gets its own tables at tenants//var/lib/runners... The exception is the fetch snapshots, which the runner writes and the control plane reads. That shared location is why a runner and its control plane must use the same tenant.
Set FACE_TENANT before an instance’s first boot. That boot copies any legacy data into the tenant it sees, once. If you set the tenant later, the legacy data stays under default-tenant. On a runner, keep RUNNER_ID stable. The operator uses the Deployment name. If it fell back to the pod name, every restart would start the runner on a fresh, empty set of tables. When there is no object store, the local root must be on storage that survives a restart. The operator points FACE_APPFS_DIR at appfs/ inside the pod’s persistent connections volume. If the default location next to face.db were used instead, it would be on the /data emptyDir, and sessions and credentials would be lost on every restart.
Sessions are validated on every request against this root, with a 2-second cache. A revocation on the control plane therefore takes effect on a runner within that window.
data.what-to-back-up#What to back up: The core-envelope-kek Secret, escrowed offline. The object-store buckets FACE writes to: the face appfs bucket, the bucket in OBJECTSTORE_BUCKET, and the Litestream replica bucket. When there is no object store: the node-local connections volume, which contains the appfs root, and the knowledge directory. The node-local /raft volume, which holds the control plane’s consensus state (RAFT_DATA_DIR). To restore, put the KEK Secret back first, then the object-store data, and only then start the control plane. The restore init container rebuilds face.db from the replica.

data:
FACE has four boot-time requirements. The order they are satisfied in matters. Each one must be present in the target namespace before you roll an image that requires it. If the image goes first, the pod crashloops instead of starting. A crashloop is the designed outcome, because an operator sees it within the first minute. Still, it is an outage you can avoid by landing the deployment side first.
Requirement Supplied as Where it comes from Session signing key AUTH_JWT_SECRET The face-session Secret. The runink operator creates it if it is absent. Shared mesh CA MESH_CA_CERT, MESH_CA_KEY The core-mesh-ca Secret, distributed with core mesh ca --namespace . At-rest key encryption key (KEK) CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK The core-envelope-kek Secret. The operator creates it if it is absent and never overwrites it. Inference endpoint INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL Set by the operator, or in your resource’s env. The three secrets are read through the platform secret backend (SECRET_BACKEND). With the default env backend, they come from the environment. With SECRET_BACKEND=file, they come from files in SECRETS_DIR (default /var/run/secrets), and the environment is the fallback. A file may be named exactly like the variable (AUTH_JWT_SECRET) or in lower case with dashes (auth-jwt-secret).
data.confirm-the-inference-endpoint#Confirm t: kubectl -n set env deploy/ --list | grep INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL Then prove the endpoint answers. See Model plane.
data.confirm-the-kek-and-session-secrets#Conf: kubectl -n get secret core-envelope-kek face-session When the operator reconciles a ControlPlane, it creates both Secrets if they are missing. If you provision them yourself, the KEK must be a base64-encoded 32-byte key (openssl rand -base64 32). Escrow the KEK before any data is written. See Persistence and backup.
data.distribute-the-mesh-ca#Distribute the me: core mesh ca --namespace kubectl -n get secret core-mesh-ca -o jsonpath='{.data.MESH_CA_CERT}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates The Secret needs both keys, and the CA must be inside its validity window. An expired CA fails the same way a missing one does, and restarting the pod does not help: redistribute the CA first.
data.roll-the-image#Roll the image: Only now roll the FACE image. See Upgrades and CD.
data.the-fatal-at-boot-checks#The fatal-at-bo:
These checks run in runServer in the order shown. Each one ends the process with the message quoted, followed by guidance text that is not reproduced here.
1. Session signing key. This runs first, before the port is bound.
❌ refusing to serve: face has no session signing key configured (AUTH_JWT_SECRET unset) There is deliberately no generated fallback. A generated key would differ per replica, so users would be signed out whenever a request reached another pod. Outside a cluster, set AUTH_JWT_SECRET directly.
2. Mesh identity.
❌ mesh identity unavailable, refusing to start: MESH_CA_CERT: secret "MESH_CA_CERT" is not configured The same line names MESH_CA_KEY when that key is the one missing, and carries the CA loader’s error when the CA is unusable. The mesh planes (control plane to runner, raft peers, the mTLS half of the app port) are never served in cleartext. No setting of any variable turns this check off.
3. Embedding format. The process exits if EMBEDDING_FORMAT names an unknown format:
EMBEDDING_FORMAT: corpus: unknown embedding format "" (known: …) 4. Inference endpoint.
no inference endpoint configured: INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL is unset or blank. FACE ships no inference binary and has no local fallback tier. This check only proves that a value is set. It does not prove that the plane is reachable, or that a model is loaded.
5. The appfs root. This is where sessions live, so FACE will not serve without it.
FACE appfs root: … envelope: at-rest KEK unavailable: CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK: secret "CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK" is not configured Check the Secret is projected: kubectl -n runink-system get secret core-envelope-kek The wrapped part depends on the backend. With no object store it is appfs: refusing to mount without at-rest encryption:. With an object store it starts approot: object store configured but unavailable:. The line always starts FACE appfs root: and always ends with the KEK error.
